text: The part of your skin that you can see and touch is made of dead cells. Yet it protects your body every day. How can dead cells do that? Let's look closer.
Your skin is the largest organ of your body. It has three layers: the epidermis on top, the dermis in the middle, and the hypodermis underneath.

The epidermis is the outer layer. About ninety percent of its cells are keratinocytes, which make keratin, a tough protein. New cells form at the bottom and are pushed upward. The outermost cells are dead, flat and filled with keratin.
That is the answer to the mystery. Layers of dead, keratin-filled cells form a protective membrane. They are constantly shed and replaced from below, so your body always has a fresh barrier.

At the bottom of the epidermis are melanocytes. They make melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color. Sunlight makes them produce more melanin, which absorbs ultraviolet light like a built-in sunscreen.
Below it is the dermis. It holds collagen and elastin fibers that give the skin strength and stretch. It also contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles, sweat glands and oil glands.
Sweat glands release sweat, and as it evaporates, it helps cool you down. Sebaceous glands make sebum, an oily substance that helps waterproof your skin and hair.
The hypodermis is the deepest layer. It stores fat, which cushions and insulates your body.
Your skin also helps make vitamin D. When ultraviolet light from the sun reaches the skin, it converts a cholesterol-related molecule into vitamin D3.

Remember three things. Skin has three layers: the epidermis, the dermis and the hypodermis. The outer layer is dead cells that protect you, and they are constantly replaced. And skin does more than cover you: it senses, cools, waterproofs and helps make vitamin D. If you have a concern about your skin, talk to a doctor.
